Female Shanny (Stichaeus grigorjewi) attain an ultimate total length of 60 centimeters [Li = 60 centimeters], a size that distinguishes them as one of the larger members of the Stichaeidae family. Field surveys conducted in the Sea of Japan indicate that individuals typically reach this maximum dimension after several years of sustained growth. The species exhibits a pronounced sexual size dimorphism, with females consistently exceeding males in both length and body mass. This pattern of female-biased size advantage is relatively uncommon among boreal littoral fishes and is thought to be linked to the energetic demands of egg production in cold-water environments. Under the ambient thermal regime of their natural habitat, which averages 1.8 °C [T = 1.8 °C], females achieve a wet weight at birth of 0.0026 grams [Wwb = 0.0026 grams], a value derived from the egg diameter of the closely related congener Stichaeus punctatus. This initial mass is remarkably small, emphasizing the highly altricial state of the newly emerged yolk-sac larva, which must rapidly commence exogenous feeding to fuel its subsequent development and growth through the pelagic larval phase.

Reproductive maturation in female Shanny occurs at a total length at puberty of 30 centimeters [Lp = 30 centimeters], a size that corresponds to the onset of vitellogenesis and the ability to produce competent oocytes. This length threshold is reached after a prolonged juvenile period spent foraging among rocky subtidal substrates and consuming small benthic invertebrates. At this critical size, the estimated wet weight at puberty is 145.7 grams [Wwp = 145.7 grams], a value that aligns well with the general length-weight relationship described for this species and provides a useful metric for assessing reproductive readiness in field-caught individuals. Puberty is not solely a function of size, however, as water temperature exerts a strong modulating influence on gonadal recrudescence. In their cold-water environment, the progression from immature juvenile to the first breeding adult is a gradual process, ensuring that females have accumulated sufficient somatic reserves to support the energetic costs of spawning before engaging in their first reproductive event.

The maximum lifespan documented for Stichaeus grigorjewi is 17 years [am = 17 years] when measured at a stable water temperature of 1.8 °C [T = 1.8 °C], a longevity estimate based on comparative data from the congeneric species Stichaeus punctatus. This extended lifespan is notable for a teleost inhabiting seasonally variable high-latitude coastal waters and positions the Shanny as a relatively slow-lived, iteroparous species that reproduces across multiple breeding seasons. The cold thermal regime likely contributes to this long adult duration by reducing metabolic rates and slowing the accumulation of oxidative cellular damage over time. This extended life span also has important consequences for population dynamics, as it allows for multiple spawning events by older, larger females, which tend to produce clutches of higher fecundity and greater larval viability. The maximum lifespan of approximately 6,205 days [am = approximately 6,205 days] underscores a life-history strategy that emphasizes adult survival and repeated reproductive effort over a single, high-investment breeding event at a temperature of 1.8 °C [T = 1.8 °C].

Females that have attained adulthood exhibit a substantial maximum body size, with the ultimate female wet weight reaching 1,300 grams [Wwi = 1,300 grams]. This impressive mass is attained through a prolonged period of somatic growth that continues well after the onset of sexual maturity. The relationship between length and weight in this species follows a typical allometric scaling pattern, with the ultimate female wet weight being a direct consequence of the maximum attainable length. In terms of daily reproductive output, a large female measuring 11 centimeters in total length produces approximately 255 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 255 eggs per day] when experiencing a stable water temperature of 1.8 °C [T = 1.8 °C]. This daily spawning rate, equivalent to roughly 0.7 eggs per day [Ri = roughly 0.7 eggs per day] averaged across the year, reflects the intermittent batch-spawning pattern typical of cold-water stichaeids, where oocyte batches are released over several weeks to maximize larval survival under fluctuating prey availability. The reproductive rate is not static, however, and is highly sensitive to variations in both female body size and local thermal conditions, with larger, older females contributing disproportionately to the total egg production of the population.

Comparative physiological studies reveal that the early life stages of Stichaeus grigorjewi are characterized by an extremely small initial mass, and this pattern of reproductive investment extends to the adult stage as well. At eclosion, the newly emerged yolk-sac larva possesses an extremely low body mass of only 0.0026 grams [Wwb = 0.0026 grams], representing the minimal energetic endowment provided by the egg at the moment of chorion rupture. The 5-orders-of-magnitude difference between this birth mass and the ultimate female wet weight of 1,300 grams [Wwi = 1,300 grams] underscores the extreme ontogenetic niche shift from a planktonic larva to a benthic predator, a trajectory sustained over a life span exceeding 17 years [am = 17 years] in the cold waters of the northern Pacific continental shelf at a temperature of 1.8 °C [T = 1.8 °C]. The transition from a lecithotrophic larva to an exogenously feeding pelagic larva is a critical bottleneck, and the small size at this stage places a premium on the rapid development of feeding structures and swimming capabilities.
